name: Body language / presence training
lead: Body language or presence training is the deliberate practice of nonverbal behaviour, such as an open stance, steady eye contact and slower movements, intended to make a person appear more confident or commanding. It is discussed in appearance communities alongside posture and grooming.

Wikipedia defines body language as nonverbal communication through posture, gestures, facial expressions, eye movement, touch and use of space, mostly occurring without conscious awareness.[1] Research on whether trained postures change outcomes is contested: the "power posing" literature found a reliable effect on feelings but no reliable effect on hormones, and an unclear effect on behaviour.[2]
infobox: Open stance, eye contact, slower movements

paras: The study of body movement in communication is called kinesics. Ray Birdwhistell, who developed it, held that gestures are polysemic and cannot be decoded in any absolute way, and rejected the term "body language".[1] Edward T. Hall introduced proxemics in 1966, defining intimate, personal, social and public distance zones.[1]

Reports note that leaning forward and nodding suggests openness, folded arms are often read as a closed mind, and relaxed hands suggest confidence.[1] Eye contact is often read as sincerity in workplaces, but meaning varies by culture, with prolonged gaze seen as a challenge or anger in some cultures.[1] The same gesture can differ in meaning: arms akimbo may signal relaxed confidence in Western countries but is considered rude in Bali.[1]

In 2010 Dana Carney, Amy Cuddy and Andy Yap reported that holding expansive poses changed hormone levels in 42 participants, and Cuddy popularised the idea in a 2012 TED talk.[2] A 2015 replication by Eva Ranehill and colleagues found an effect on felt power but not on hormones, risk tolerance or behaviour.[2] Carney stated in 2016 that she no longer believed the effect was real, while Cuddy and colleagues published a 2018 meta-analysis of 55 studies reporting evidential value for effects on feelings.[2] A 2022 meta-analysis of 128 studies reported reliable effects on thoughts and feelings, no effect on physiological measures and an unclear behavioural effect, with few studies including a neutral-posture control.[2]

Scholars disagree whether body language is universal, and Mehrabian's often-cited 7%-38%-55% split is widely debated.[1] Wikipedia states there is no scientific evidence that nonverbal cues reliably detect lies.[1]
No studies found for presence training as a looks-related intervention. Related laboratory research on power posing is summarised above.[2]

timeline.event: Carney, Cuddy and Yap publish the original power-posing study.[2]
Ranehill and colleagues report a larger replication without hormone or behaviour effects.[2]
Carney states she no longer believes the effect is real.[2]
Körner and colleagues publish a 128-study meta-analysis.[2]

card.summary: Training stance, eye contact and pace to look more confident; the research supports felt confidence more than outcomes.
card.note: Meanings of gestures vary by culture; power-posing hormone effects were not replicated.

quick.overview:
Body language training means practising open posture, steady eye contact and calmer movement to project confidence.

Power-posing research found reliable effects on how people feel, but not on hormones, and behavioural effects are unclear. Gesture meanings also vary across cultures.
quick.mechanism: Practitioners say changing outward behaviour alters how others read confidence and may feed back into mood. Studies support the mood link more than the others.
quick.risks: Low risk. Cross-cultural misreading of gestures and eye contact is the main caveat noted in references.
